newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Geneva talks seek global pollution pact.
newsitem.headline: Geneva talks seek global pollution pact.

text.p: Negotiators from more than 150 countries began talks in Geneva on Monday to seek a binding pact on reducing air pollution blamed for health problems.

At the eight-day conference, more than 700 delegates will negotiate details of a stack of proposals to reduce gas emissions from oil and coal which could affect the future consumption of energy from house-heating to public transport.
But participants said a breakthrough was unlikely amid continuing wrangling over voluntary or mandatory targets that has held back progress over the past year.

"The details being negotiated will affect our lives. They will affect prices of energy and retail fuel consumption from public transport to cars," Michael Williams of the U.N. Climate Convention Secretariat said.
"But the negotiations will be inconclusive. The chances of agreeing on a consolidated single text may be worse than 50-50," he added.

Most industries, in particular those involving fossil fuels, and exporting countries oppose the global warming and air standards proposals to reduce gas emissions from oil and coal, saying they would force expensive pollution controls on businesses and motor vehicles and would weaken the economy.

The latest negotiations of the United Nations Conference on Climate Change follow an earlier round in July. The talks aim to conclude a final pact to be presented to a meeting next December in Kyoto, Japan. The next round will be in February in Bonn.
The proposals negotiated in Geneva, some tougher than others, are on how much greenhouse gas emissions should be cut and by what deadline, such as 2005, 2010 or 2020.
Coal exporters such as Australia, many OPEC countries which fear oil consumption cuts will hit their economies and heavy industry groups could resist the targets, diplomats say.
The United States, in a paper to be offered at the Geneva talks, will propose making 2010 the first deadline to meet targets in cutting industrial emissions, diplomats said.
Williams said the 15-nation European Union and many other countries were also leaning towards deadlines later than 2005.
U.S. environmentalists have criticised the U.S. proposals as a sluggish response to global warming, saying the offering could undermine a treaty.
